title: Norms, Surprises, and Causes
hook: The proofing racks are flat at dawn, and the first story blames the night baker before the dough is touched.
counterintuition: Surprise does not just make you curious. It pressures the mind to restore order with a cause, so the better move is to separate the broken expectation from the story you are tempted to invent.
tryThisNow: The next time something breaks pattern, write two lines: expected, observed. Only then write the possible cause and one fact that would test it.
keyTakeaway: When a norm breaks, pause before assigning cause; identify the expectation first, then test whether the tempting explanation actually fits.

breakdown.fastRead:
A bakery manager opens the proofing room at 5:10 a.m. and sees three racks sitting flat. The expectation was height. The surprise is collapse. The first cause appears instantly: the night baker rushed the yeast.

That story may be right.

It may also be the mind patching a broken norm too fast. Surprise asks for a cause, and the cause often arrives as blame, intent, or a neat story. Split the event: what did I expect, what cause am I adding, and what check would link the two?
breakdown.deepRead:
A tax fraud reviewer sees a refund claim that is twice the usual size for that filer. The worksheet does not feel merely large. It feels suspicious. That feeling comes from a violated norm: this filer usually claims less.

Surprise is a demand for order.

The mind is skilled at norms. It learns what usually follows what, who normally does which thing, how a room should sound, how a form should look, how a machine should behave. When the pattern breaks, attention snaps to the break and searches for cause. The search often leans toward intentionality because intention is a satisfying explanation. Someone hid income. Someone cut a corner. Someone ignored the warning.

The problem is not that causes are fake. Causes matter. The problem is that the first cause often appears before the violated expectation has been named clearly. If the expectation was wrong, stale, or too narrow, the causal story is built on sand. A larger refund could come from fraud, but also from a new child, corrected withholding, a one-time credit, or a prior filing error. Until the reviewer separates surprise from accusation, the cause will feel stronger than the evidence.

A rare-books desk gives a smaller version. A manuscript arrives with a cradle strap loosened, and the librarian feels someone mishandled it. The violated norm is tight support. The tempting cause is careless visitor. But the humidity log shows the binding expanded overnight. The surprise was real. The blame was invented too fast.

Name the violation before naming the villain.
breakdown.fullRead:
You notice norms constantly without announcing them. The train usually arrives from the left. A colleague usually answers in two sentences. A supplier usually sends twelve cases, not eleven. Most of the time, the norm sits in the background. Then something breaks it, and the mind goes looking for why.

A factory quality cage makes the sequence visible. The caliper inspection tag labeled violation shows a batch whose measurements are suddenly off center. The supervisor expects ordinary variation around the target. Instead the pieces cluster high. Within seconds, someone says the operator must have adjusted the machine to save time. That may be true. But the surprise has already recruited intentionality before the tooling log, material lot, and calibration record have been checked.

What was violated: the measurement pattern. What was invented: a motive. Those are not the same thing.

This distinction matters because causal stories feel like relief. A broken norm is uncomfortable. A cause closes the loop. The loop can close around a real mechanism, or around a story that only satisfies the discomfort. People are especially quick to see intention because intentions make messy events legible. The late shipment becomes disrespect. The missed email becomes avoidance. The broken part becomes negligence. Sometimes those readings are right. Often they are merely available.

The correction is not to suspend all causal thinking. That would be useless. Work requires cause: tax reviewers need to find fraud, avalanche forecasters need to explain weak layers, bakers need to identify bad proofing, repair shops need to find the failed part. The better discipline is sequence. First identify the norm. Second state the observed violation. Third list at least two possible causes, including one that does not require blame or intention. Fourth check the evidence that would distinguish them.

A neon sign repair shop can use this sequence in ten seconds. The tube flickers only when the client stands near the counter, and the apprentice wants to blame rough handling during pickup. The supervisor circles the dramatic detail, client nearby, then crosses it out until the boring comparison is done: transformer output, ground, tube temperature, and switch position. If the client caused it, the checks will show the path. If not, the story was only surprise wearing a face.

A library rare-books desk uses the same sequence with quieter stakes. A cradle strap is loose; loose means risk; risk invites a culprit. The handler may be careless. Or the binding may have shifted. Or the prior strap position may have been wrong. Separating violated expectation from cause keeps preservation from becoming accusation.

The limit is that some surprises demand immediate action. If a machine sparks, you do not hold a seminar on norms before cutting power. But after the immediate safety move, the same discipline returns. Do not let the emergency story become the investigation. The first cause that calms the mind may not be the cause that explains the event.

Surprise points to a broken expectation. It does not hand you the cause.

examples.title: Beth separates refund from fraud

planSpec.domain: tax fraud review unit facing a decision distorted by expectation
planSpec.audience: a lead or reviewer who must pause after surprise and separate the violated expectation from the cause you are tempted to invent while others want the quick answer
planSpec.stakes: the visible call will go wrong unless expectation is separated from the tempting but weaker cue
planSpec.requiredBeat: the scene shows the before call written on the tax audit worksheet labeled norms, then the after call once the person performs the correction instead of trusting the original feeling

examples.scenario: "That cannot be the whole answer," Beth says, with the tax audit worksheet labeled norms between refund and fraud. A filer who usually claims small refunds is asking for twice the prior amount. Before review, Beth would have marked suspicious. After writing expected refund and observed refund in separate boxes, she sees new dependent and withholding change. She must decide whether surprise alone gets to become a fraud cause.
examples.whatToDo: Write the violated expectation first, then check filing changes, credits, withholding, and prior-year corrections before assigning fraud risk.
examples.whyItMatters: The large refund violates a norm, but violation is not cause. The separate boxes prevent surprise from turning directly into accusation.

questions.prompt: A tax reviewer sees a refund twice as large as a filer usually claims and immediately suspects fraud. New dependent and withholding changes are visible in the file. What should happen first?
choices: Separate the violated refund expectation from the cause and check the filing changes.
Mark the case fraud-risk because the refund violates the filer's norm.
Ignore the unusual refund because legitimate changes exist.
questions.explanation: The unusual refund is a real surprise, but fraud is only one cause. Checking dependent status and withholding tests the explanation. Marking fraud skips the separation; ignoring the refund drops the useful signal.

questions.prompt: A bakery manager finds flat racks at dawn and wants to blame the night baker. Room temperature and yeast lot have not been checked. What is the most precise diagnosis?
choices: The manager is showing healthy accountability.
A broken expectation has been converted into a personal cause too quickly.
The dough should be discarded before any cause is considered.
questions.explanation: Flat racks violate the expected rise, but the cause remains open. Blame may be right only after temperature, yeast, and mix checks. Accountability without evidence is just a satisfying story.

questions.prompt: An avalanche forecaster gets a surprising shear result and immediately blames the new snow. Wind loading and crust history are available. Which move is best?
choices: Name new snow as the cause because the shear result is urgent.
Treat all causes as equally likely until the end of the day.
State the violated expectation, then test new snow against wind loading and crust history.
questions.explanation: The weak layer needs a cause, but the first cause should compete with plausible alternatives. Urgency does not license the nearest story. Equal-likelihood paralysis ignores that evidence can distinguish causes now.

questions.prompt: A rare-books librarian finds a loose cradle strap after a visitor leaves. Humidity rose overnight and the binding may have expanded. What is the soundest response?
choices: Check humidity, prior strap position, and handling notes before assigning fault.
Assume mishandling because visitors are the most direct cause.
Avoid investigating because accusation could upset the visitor.
questions.explanation: The loose strap violates a preservation norm, but mishandling is only one cause. The environmental and handling checks distinguish mechanisms. Avoiding investigation is as weak as blaming too fast.

questions.prompt: A factory batch shifts high after lunch. A supervisor says the operator probably adjusted the machine to save time. Calibration and material-lot records are unreviewed. What is the main error?
choices: Using measurement data instead of direct observation.
Treating intentionality as the default cause for a violated measurement norm.
Considering operator action as one possible cause.
questions.explanation: The shift breaks the norm, but intentional adjustment is not proven. Calibration and material records may explain it. Considering operator action is fine; making it the default before checks is the error.

questions.prompt: A neon sign flickers when a client stands near it, and an apprentice blames the client for bumping the tube. Transformer output and grounding have not been checked. What should the supervisor do?
choices: Ask the client to leave so the sign can be tested without social pressure.
Accept the apprentice's explanation because timing is strong evidence.
Run the boring electrical checks before treating the client's presence as a cause.
questions.explanation: The timing is vivid, but electrical checks are what connect flicker to mechanism. Removing the client may help testing but does not replace the checks. Accepting the timing turns coincidence into cause.

questions.prompt: A team leader says, "When something surprises us, the first explanation is usually the right one because it comes from experience." Which reply best fits this principle?
choices: The first explanation may be useful, but it should be tested against the violated expectation and alternatives.
Experience is irrelevant once surprise appears.
Surprise should be ignored until a full investigation is complete.
questions.explanation: Experience can offer a candidate cause, but surprise also pressures premature closure. Testing the cause against alternatives preserves experience without letting it skip evidence. The other choices either reject or freeze the signal.

questions.prompt: A customer who is usually polite sends a one-word reply. The account manager assumes anger and drafts an apology. What is the better first step?
choices: Send the apology because the norm violation signals damage.
Ask what expectation was violated and what other causes could explain the short reply.
Ignore the reply until the customer sends a longer message.
questions.explanation: The one-word reply breaks a communication norm, but anger is only one cause. Time pressure, mobile typing, or simple agreement may explain it. Ignoring the message avoids the cause question rather than improving it.

questions.prompt: A software monitor shows an unusual traffic spike. The engineer immediately blames a marketing campaign, but no campaign is scheduled. Which action fits best?
choices: Assume the campaign calendar is wrong because traffic spikes usually come from marketing.
Restart the monitor before asking any cause questions.
Separate expected traffic from observed spike, then test campaign, bot, outage, and measurement explanations.
questions.explanation: The spike is the violation; campaign is only one cause. Testing several explanations avoids the first repair story. Assuming the calendar is wrong protects the first cause, while restarting may erase evidence before diagnosis.

reviewCards.front: Something breaks pattern and a cause appears instantly. What should you write first?
reviewCards.back: Write the expectation and the observation separately. Only after that should you write the possible cause and the fact that would test it.

reviewCards.front: A refund, shipment, or reply is unusual. Why is the first explanation risky?
reviewCards.back: Because surprise creates pressure to restore order. The first explanation may calm the violation before evidence connects it to the event.

reviewCards.front: A failure invites blame. What non-blame alternative should be added before deciding?
reviewCards.back: Add a mechanism that does not require intention, such as environment, measurement error, changed input, timing, or stale expectation. Then check which cause fits.

reviewCards.front: Why can intentionality appear too soon after surprise?
reviewCards.back: Intentions make broken norms feel orderly. The mind often prefers a person-shaped cause because it closes the loop quickly, even when records or measurements point elsewhere.

reviewCards.front: A machine sparks and immediate action is needed. Does the norm-cause separation still matter?
reviewCards.back: Yes, after the safety action. Cut power first, then keep the emergency story separate from the investigation so the first calming cause does not become the official cause.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is preserving the gap between surprise and cause. A violated expectation is evidence that something changed, not evidence that your first explanation is true.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a metric, file, or reply breaks its usual pattern, then write expected and observed before naming a cause.
If a symptom or reading surprises you, then list one cause involving intent or behavior and one involving environment, measurement, or timing before acting.
If a machine or process fails in an unusual way, then check input, environment, and measurement records before blaming a person.
If someone's behavior violates your expectation, then ask what expectation was broken and name two possible causes before responding.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In the next day, catch one surprise. Write expected, observed, first cause, alternate cause, and one test. Do not act on the cause until the test is named.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, review a recent surprise. Mark whether you separated the violated norm from the cause, and whether the eventual evidence supported the first story.

memorableLines.why: It keeps the correction from becoming anti-cause.

memorableLines.text: Surprise is a demand for order.
memorableLines.why: It names why causal stories arrive so quickly.

memorableLines.text: Surprise points to a broken expectation.
memorableLines.why: It gives readers the first half of the separation move.
